title: Korea–Canada Strategic Energy & Industrial Partnership
subtitle: Where deeper industrial integration creates strategic value, through which instruments, and where to stay out

inlines.v: Battery Materials & Cells: Accumulator parts & separators (Korea->Canada). Nuclear Fuel & Reactor Systems: Uranium conversion & enrichment † (Canada->Korea).

Recognise trusted partner supply of accumulator parts & separators; oil extraction; cathode materials & precursors in procurement and content rules. Keep market access open and predictable for non-oriented electrical steel (NGO), coal extraction (no new tariff on the trusted supplier). Keep nuclear special materials; battery recycling feed; semiconductor manufacturing equipment open to global sourcing.
Upgrade Critical-minerals and energy-security MOU (2023) and 2026 stockpiling track: sector strategy, reciprocal commitments, a KPI dashboard and an annual review. No new MOU.

Do not create a new bilateral energy MOU or a free-standing MEA institution. Do not put new public money behind Cathode materials & precursors investment that is already committed (evidence KRCA-17). Do not defend AC generators as a bilateral priority.

Of 117 technology x stage cells and electro-industrial nodes assessed for the pair (not counting 25 cells whose products are read node by node), 11 show an active complementarity (a supplier meeting the other's need, a shared chokepoint, a capacity-constrained trusted supplier or a chain specialisation), 0 direct competition and 82 no strategic case. The relationship is not one of general similarity: most of the electro-industrial base needs no bilateral intervention.

AIB strategic roles: Korea Specialized Technology & Manufacturing Anchor (primary), Scale Manufacturing & Integration Platform (primary), Coordination / Bridge Hub (secondary), Capital & Investment Anchor (secondary); Canada Resource & Processing Anchor (primary), Capital & Investment Anchor (secondary), Demand & Market Anchor (secondary).

Canada supplies uranium conversion & enrichment † where Korea is short; Korea supplies accumulator parts & separators, non-oriented electrical steel (NGO) where Canada is short; they share no node-level chokepoint where neither supplies; and they specialise at different steps of the same chains in cathode materials & precursors, nickel intermediates & chemicals, power cables, aluminium wire rod.

From the AIB roles, Korea brings specialised technology and manufacturing, scale manufacturing, coordination across allied chains; Canada brings resources and processing, capital, demand and offtake. Public finance runs through KEXIM, K-SURE, KOMIR, KDB on the Korea side and ISED, EDC, CIB, CGF, CMIF, FinDev on the Canada side. The trade is market access and demand certainty for trusted capacity.
(tier 1 by the rules in Section 3, one per compact; recommended compacts first, then by urgency and importance):

Accumulator parts & separators: demand and long-term offtake

Outside the electro-industrial compacts, the rules also find fuel-trade lanes (oil extraction; coal components); they are handled in the trade agenda, not as compacts.
Do not create a new bilateral energy MOU or a free-standing MEA institution: KRCA-M2 already exists (a standing framework with no pipeline or finance yet); dock the compacts in it.
Do not put new public money behind Cathode materials & precursors investment that is already committed (evidence KRCA-17); support is additional only beyond it.
Do not defend AC generators as a bilateral priority: trusted supply is adequate (AIB LOW INTERVENTION), yet Canada's observed protection or attention is high.

This section sets out what already exists before anything new is proposed. Facts are from the curated evidence layer (accessed 2026-11-17); items marked partial or unverified rest on secondary sources and should be confirmed before citation.
Canada's memberships in OSI's economic-security agreements table: G7, MSP, NATO, U.S. FTA.

Economic-security 2+2 (Joly, Champagne, Park Jin, Ahn Dukgeun) launched Sep 2022 and first met in Seoul on 16 May 2023; priorities were critical minerals, clean energy, supply chains, AI and economic coercion.

A joint statement in New York on 23 Sep 2024 set up a network of MSP export-credit agencies, development-finance institutions and state-backed funds. Its purpose is to share information, coordinate and co-finance critical-minerals projects. Named members include DFC, Export Development Canada, JICA, JBIC, KEXIM and Export Finance Norway among others.

At the 19 Feb 2026 Ministerial, IEA ministers endorsed an expanded phase of the Critical Minerals Security Programme, which was established in 2022. The expansion covers: support for members that set up or expand stockpiles; rapid market assessments and coordinated responses during supply disruptions; regular table-top exercises (a rare-earth exercise was held in Nov 2025); a wider information dashboard; a new Technology Collaboration Programme on recycling and substitution. The release gives no budget.

Second 2+2 (first was Nov 2024) agreed to pursue an update of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Action Plan, start Defence Cooperation Agreement steps and coordinate on economic security; the statement does not mention critical minerals or energy; next meeting in Korea in 2028.

On 2 Jun 2026 Canada and Korea agreed to develop a joint critical-minerals stockpiling plan by end-2026, discussed strategic-resource investments, and Korea agreed to facilitate CKFTA preferential tariffs for Canadian crude; no volumes or amounts given.

Lee and Carney agreed on 16 Jun 2026 to strengthen cooperation in defence, security, energy and critical minerals; an informal meeting followed at the NATO summit; no deliverables or amounts reported.

On 7 Oct 2026 the trade ministers of Argentina, Australia, Canada, the EU, France, Germany, India, Italy, Japan, Korea, Mexico, Poland, Turkiye, the UK and the US signed a statement committing to new sectoral platforms on structural excess capacity. The platforms start with autos and EVs, batteries, chemicals, foundational semiconductors and solar panels, and officials are to meet at technical level before December 2026 to draft terms of reference and share data.
In the OSI energy basket, Korea imported US$3.7bn from Canada and Canada imported US$3.4bn from Korea (bilateral flows 2024, summed over the technology x stage cells).

Signed in Ottawa 22 Sep 2014 and in force 1 Jan 2015; Canada's first FTA in Asia-Pacific, covering goods, services, investment and procurement; nearly 90% of Canadian exports to Korea duty-free at entry into force.
From 26 Dec 2025 Canada cut FTA-partner steel quotas to 75% of 2024 volumes with a 50% over-quota surtax; Korea protested that this breaches the CKFTA and sought an exemption, none found.
The Comprehensive Strategic Partnership was launched in 2022 and is the base for the Jan 2026 industrial MOU; leaders agreed in Sep 2022 to develop a critical-minerals and energy MOU.

Non-binding MOU (2023, not 2022) covering critical-mineral value chains, clean fuels and CCS, and clean-energy, ZEV and semiconductor manufacturing, with an action plan and investment-screening cooperation; it lets Korea count Canada toward the US EV-credit minerals test.

Carney and Lee welcomed the partnership at the Gyeongju APEC summit on 30 Oct 2025, Canada's first in the Indo-Pacific, and finalised a classified-information agreement that supports defence procurement; the readout does not mention energy, critical minerals or LNG.

Joly and Korea's Trade, Industry and Resources Minister Kim Jung-kwan signed in Ottawa; sets up an industrial cooperation committee and a forum on a Korean auto footprint, battery production, materials processing and critical-minerals recycling; no amounts or companies named.

The Geological Survey of Canada and Korea's KIGAM signed an implementation agreement on naturally occurring hydrogen research and development, announced with the 2 Jun 2026 energy and critical-minerals meeting.

As of 9 Nov 2026 the ~C$100m (US$73m) build is on budget with C$59.3m of government contributions (including a C$20m federal agreement of 4 May 2026 and C$17.5m from Ontario); early commissioning is targeted for Q4 2026 and commercial production for 2H 2027, at 5,120 t/yr contained cobalt, with about 60% committed to LG Energy Solution.

Where the findings are weak or counterintuitive
Joint bets resting on a node need inherited from its cell (a proxy): Accumulator parts & separators; Uranium conversion & enrichment †.
Evidence-led compacts (OSI cannot see the partner's capability in trade data): none.

Canada has no listed trade position (under 1% of world supply) at nodes where Korea has material demand: wafers, polysilicon, synthetic graphite (anode-grade), rare-earth oxides & compounds, electric motors, rare-earth permanent magnets, lithium chemicals, PV cover glass, refrigerants, battery materials (foil, electrolyte), battery recycling feed, graphite electrodes, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, silver powder, direct-reduced iron (DRI/HBI). Trade data miss capability that is owned abroad or sold at home, so these nodes cannot show complementarity even where corporate evidence suggests it.
Product-definition caveats (†) at 1 node: the notes are under the Section 2 node table.
Low-evidence units among the active states: none.

Trade data understate concentration at uranium conversion & enrichment †: enrichment is sold as a service under long-term contracts, so goods trade understates Russia's share of world enrichment capacity (roughly 40%), and the 2024 US ban on Russian low-enriched uranium imports makes trusted capacity the binding constraint.

Trade data understate concentration at gallium, germanium & indium: China's export controls since 2023 cut its recorded exports, so 2024 trade understates its share of primary gallium and germanium output (the large majority of world supply).

Fuel-trade lanes reach tier 1 (oil extraction; coal components; buyer: Korea and Canada): real energy-security lanes, but outside the electro-industrial compacts and with no market failure beyond the supply concentration the engine measures.

inlines.v: Uranium/fuel Extraction: aggregated low-coverage sub-sectors (Spent fuel & nuclear scrap, Uranium ores)

Keep Canada exports of Uranium conversion & enrichment to Korea tariff-free and predictable, but confirm the supplier's actual capability first: trade data understate concentration at this node (Section 11).
Recognise Korea output of Accumulator parts & separators as trusted domestic-equivalent supply in Canada procurement and content rules; capacity, not access, is the constraint.
Recognise Canada output of Oil extraction as trusted domestic-equivalent supply in Korea procurement and content rules; capacity, not access, is the constraint.
Keep Korea exports of Coal components to Canada tariff-free and predictable; the buyer's need is met by the trusted supplier.
